Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Therapy Content: avoid thinking about anything discussed in therapy, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Vignette:
Connor was nineteen, a counselor at a residential treatment center for adolescents, and he had been with his girlfriend, Maya, for just over a year when his life was interrupted by a fever that would not break. What started as a persistent flu-like illness escalated over three days into septic shock, a life-threatening cascade that landed him in the intensive care unit for a week. He remembered the moment the emergency room doctor inserted the first IV—a thick-gauge needle sliding into the crook of his arm—and the way his mother’s face had crumpled when the crash cart was wheeled in. He remembered the antiseptic smell that clung to every breath, the beeping of monitors that seemed to count down rather than count up, and the terrifying sensation of his own body turning against him: his heart racing uncontrollably, his skin mottling, his limbs trembling as if they belonged to someone else. The medical team had saved his life, but Connor had come to believe that his body was no longer his ally. It had betrayed him once, and he was certain it would do so again.

In the months following his discharge, Connor returned to work, but the treatment center became a minefield. The building smelled faintly of cleaning solution, a scent that triggered a visceral lurch in his stomach and a sudden, cold sweat. He began to avoid the infirmary entirely, taking circuitous routes through the hallways to bypass it. When a client mentioned a routine blood draw, Connor felt his own pulse spike, his chest tightening as if the needle were approaching his own arm. He started staying late at the office, not out of dedication, but because he could not bring himself to go home and lie still in the dark. Sleep had become a battleground: every time he began to drift off, a sudden movement from Maya beside him—a shift, a sigh—would jolt him upright, his heart hammering, his hands shaking, convinced for a split second that he was back in the ICU, that a nurse was about to insert another line. He would stay awake until two or three in the morning, scrolling through his phone, delaying the inevitable moment when he would have to surrender to a body he no longer trusted.

His relationship with Maya began to fray. She would reach for him in bed, and he would flinch, startling at her touch. He could see the hurt in her eyes, but he could not explain that his body was reacting to a threat that had already passed, that it treated every unexpected movement as a potential assault. He had come to believe that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. The work he had once loved—helping teenagers navigate their own traumas—now felt hollow. He found himself avoiding any discussion of therapy content with his colleagues, steering conversations away from clinical topics, because talking about fear or helplessness brought him too close to his own. He stopped attending supervision meetings, claiming scheduling conflicts, because the mere mention of a patient’s medical history sent his heart racing.

What finally brought Connor to seek help was a single incident during a routine physical exam required for his job. The doctor had barely touched his arm with a stethoscope, and Connor had jerked away, his breath coming in gasps, his vision tunneling. He had excused himself to the bathroom and stood gripping the sink, staring at his own pale face in the mirror, and felt a profound, sickening certainty: his body was not just unreliable—it was his enemy. It kept reacting as if he were still in that hospital bed, still fighting for his life, even though he was safe. He could not keep living this way, jumping at shadows, avoiding his own girlfriend’s touch, dreading the smell of hand sanitizer. He was afraid that if he did not find a way to stop the cycle, he would lose his job, his relationship, and any sense of a future. He hoped, vaguely, that talking about it might help him reclaim a life that felt like his own again.
